newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - API stocks show gasoline season still strong.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - API stocks show gasoline season still strong.

text.p: REUTER POLL FORECAST* ACTUAL STOCKS FOR
FOR WEEK ENDED 08/15/97 WEEK ENDED 08/15/97-CHANGE
DISTILLATE...... UP 1.50 MLN 123,205 UP 2.460 MLN
GASOLINE........ DN 1.50 MLN 187,792 DN 3.270 MLN
UTILIZATION..... UP 0.50 PCT PT 97.5 UP 2.50 PCT PT
*NB - The forecast is derived by polling at least six market analysts, omitting the high and low forecast from and averaging the rest.
The latest weekly status report from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday shows that gasoline's 1997 summer season remains strong, though there are clouds on the horizon, analysts said.
The report showed another big drop in gasoline stocks in the week ended August 15, which were down 3.3 million barrels at just under 188 million barrels, just above a record low.
Gasoline "implied demand", which factors imports, production and the inventory move, was running at 8.836 million barrels per day (bpd) last week, still near its peak, the API data showed.
Domestic production slipped marginally to 7.883 million bpd despite a sharp jump in refinery utilization, though gasoline imports made up some of the shortfall rising 486,000 bpd.
"This is not going to make life any easier for people short of gasoline. New York area gasoline is still going at a hefty premium," said Tim Evans, a market analyst at Pegasus Econometrics.
The main market impact is likley to be another strong rise in wholesale gasoline prices in relation to crude, already at very robust levels well past their usual summer peak, said Evans.
"We are likely to get one more bullish report (for gasoline) as we approach the holiday weekend. It will be the last hurrah for gasoline," said Richard Redash, an analyst at Prudential Securities.

Analysts see in the report the seeds of an softer crude and petroleum products market as the seasonal focus shifts from the "summer driving season" to the "winter heating oil season," expected after the Labor Day weekend in early September.
Tuesday's report showed another big rise in heating oil and deisel (distillates), which were up 2.46 million barrels at 123 millin barrels, about 17 million barrels above the same time last year.
Crude oil stocks also posted a strong gain of nearly 4.8 million barrels to stand at 316 million barrels, nearly eight million barrels above last year's level.
"Crude stocks are certainly bearish," said Evans.

"It is amazing that over the last four to five weeks we've been seeing a fairly consistent pattern of crude stocks being overall bearish and gasoline just wants no part of that. But (gasoline demand) does have a tendency to drop off sharply after the Labor Day weekend," Evans added.

Indeed, the drop off in gasoline demand in September is usually by far the biggest, on average some four to five percent, said Stanley Givens, an analyst at Energy Security Analysis Inc in Washington D.C.
"I would expect that increases in crude and distillate will outweigh the drop in gasoline as we go forward," said Givens.
--((Tony McAuley, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1623))
